tour.title: Jongmyo, Gwangjang & the Cheonggye: The Old Capital on Foot
tour.summary: A winter walk through the old heart of Seoul — a shrine where Korea's kings are still ritually fed, the market that has fried mung-bean pancakes since 1905, lanes of 1920s hanok houses, and a stream dug out from under a motorway.
tour.overviewText:
Two forces made this corner of Seoul, and they are still arguing over it: Confucian duty to the dead, and the market price of a mung-bean pancake. This walk begins at a shrine where Korea's kings are still ritually fed and ends at a stream the city dug out from under a motorway, which is more or less the whole story of Seoul in under five kilometres.

From 1392 to 1910 Korea was ruled by the Joseon dynasty, a state built on Confucianism — less a religion of gods than an ethics of family and duty, with filial piety at its centre: the obligation to honour your parents in life and keep attending to them after death. Joseon applied that to the throne. Dead kings and queens became spirit tablets enshrined in Jongmyo, the royal ancestral shrine, and the living king walked there to report to his ancestors in person. Jongmyo is the oldest and most complete Confucian royal shrine anywhere, which is why UNESCO listed it in 1995; the ritual still performed there, the Jongmyo Jerye, is separately protected as living human heritage.

Around that court grew a city that had to eat. Gwangjang Market opened in 1905, the year Japan began closing its grip on Korea, founded by Korean merchants who pooled their own money to build a market Japanese capital did not control. It has traded in the same place ever since, and the people frying, rolling and serving in its alleys are overwhelmingly older women. What an old market means to a rich, fast city is one of the arguments you will walk through here.

So is the stream. The Cheonggyecheon was a waterway, then a sewer, then a concrete highway; in 2003 the city demolished the elevated road above it and reopened the water in 2005. The project made its mayor, Lee Myung-bak, president two years later. Supporters call it renewal; critics count the cost, the water pumped in to keep it flowing, and the market traders moved out to make it happen.

The walk itself drifts west through old Seoul: from the shrine, east into the market for lunch, back through lanes of hanok — traditional Korean courtyard houses, timber under heavy tiled roofs — then down and along the water to the palace gate. Winter is the right season for it: the alleys steam, the stream runs cold and clear, and something hot to eat is never far away.

Practicals: the route is about four and a half kilometres, flat and unhurried, and only Jongmyo charges an entry fee (around 1,000 won; check at the gate). Jongmyo closes on Tuesdays, and on weekdays you can only enter with a guided tour, so time your morning around that. The market's food alleys open daily; the fabric halls do not. Sun sets around 17:20 in early January, so eat early and finish in the lights, and know that the pavements, the hanok lanes and the streamside steps all ice over — wear shoes you trust. Every price and hour in Seoul moves; treat the numbers in this walk as signposts and verify them where you stand.
tour.difficulty: Easy and mostly flat, in short legs rather than long stretches; the effort is the cold and the crowds, not hills. Surfaces are the obstacle: Jongmyo's paths are packed earth and gravel, Ikseon-dong's alleys are tight and uneven, and the streamside walkway has steps and can ice over. Wear grippy shoes and allow a full day with stops and meals.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at Jongmyo by 10:00 — on weekdays that is the first English guided tour, and the shrine is quietest in the morning. Eat at Gwangjang Market around lunchtime or early afternoon, when the griddles are hottest. Aim to reach the Cheonggyecheon and Gwanghwamun Square after dark, when the stream lights and the square's winter illuminations come on. In late December and early January the sun sets around 17:20, so do not leave the market too late.

stops.name: Jongmyo Shrine
stops.narration:
This may be the quietest few hectares in central Seoul. You are inside Jongmyo, the royal ancestral shrine of the Joseon dynasty. King Taejo, the dynasty's founder, moved his capital to this valley in 1394 and work on the shrine began the same year. Confucianism is an ethics of family and duty, centred on filial piety. Joseon applied that duty to the throne, so dead kings and queens became spirit tablets, and the living king reported to his ancestors. UNESCO listed the shrine in 1995 as the oldest and most complete Confucian royal ancestral shrine anywhere.

Jeongjeon runs 101 metres across 25 bays, the longest traditional wooden building in Korea. Its 19 chambers hold 49 spirit tablets, for 19 kings and 30 queens. No gold, no paint, no statues: the virtue performed here is restraint. A king's tablet entered the main hall only after a three-year mourning period and only if the court judged his reign fit; two kings failed that test and were never enshrined, Yeonsangun and Gwanghaegun. In 1592 Japanese armies burned the shrine, but a commoner hid the tablets, and the hall was rebuilt in 1608 and extended four times.

On the first Sunday of May the Jongmyo Jerye, the royal ancestral rite, is performed before descendants of the royal family, with a court orchestra and 64 dancers in eight lines representing yin and yang. The road on the west side was cut through by the Japanese colonial government in the early twentieth century specifically to sever the geomantic "vein" between Jongmyo and the palaces. Jongmyo closes every Tuesday and, from November to January, shuts at 17:30 with last entry at 16:30; the ticket is about 1,000 won, and free-admission days are multiplying. Weekdays are guided-tour only, with English tours at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00. The paths are packed earth and gravel, so this stop is not step-free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Adults around 1,000 ₩; under 19s and over 64s are usually free with ID. A combined ticket covering Jongmyo and four palaces is also sold. Prices and free days change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Closed Tuesdays (if Tuesday is a public holiday, it closes the next day). November to January roughly 09:00–17:30, last entry 16:30; longer hours in the warmer months. On weekdays entry is by guided tour only — English at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00. Confirm the day's timetable on arrival.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free, honestly. The paths are packed earth and gravel with some uneven ground and a long walk between halls; wheelchairs and strollers struggle on the loose surface. The guided route is mostly level otherwise.
stops.insiderTip: On a cold weekday, arrive by 09:50 and join the 10:00 English tour — you get the whole shrine walking with a guide for the price of the ticket, and you are back out with the rest of the day still ahead of you. Look for the two kings missing from the main hall's tablets.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the shrine by the main gate, walk down to the wide street (Jongno) and turn right, heading east. Follow Jongno for about ten minutes, past Jongno 4-ga, to Jongno 5-ga. The covered entrance to Gwangjang Market is on your right, roughly opposite subway exit 8.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gwangjang Market
stops.narration:
This is Korea's oldest permanent market, founded in 1905 and trading in the same block ever since. It began as economic self-defence: in 1905 Japanese capital had taken over the older Namdaemun market, so a group of Korean merchants, the records name Kim Jong-han among them, pooled around 100,000 won, bought this land and opened a market Japanese investors did not control. They called it Dongdaemun Market; Gwangjang came later, from the two bridges it sits between, Gwanggyo and Janggyo. Most Korean markets then opened once every three or five days, and this one opened every day, the first to do so.

Fabric, hanbok (traditional Korean dress), bedding and household goods fill the wholesale halls; the food alleys run below. Thousands of shops and around twenty thousand people work in this 42,000-square-metre block. Three dishes bring people across the city. Bindaetteok is a thick pancake of soaked, stone-ground mung beans with pork, kimchi, bean sprouts and bracken (a wild fern shoot), dipped in soy sauce with raw onion. Mayak gimbap, "narcotic gimbap," is a joke with no drugs in it: bite-sized rolls of pickled radish and carrot in sesame oil with a sharp mustard-soy dip; the name stuck around 2012 when a blogger called one stall's rolls addictive. Yukhoe, Korean beef tartare with sesame oil and raw egg yolk, has its own alley of specialists.

In late 2025 a video alleging overcharging, a dish listed at 8,000 won billed at 10,000, damaged the whole market. Stalls must now post weights or quantities next to prices, and there is a multilingual QR complaint system; since 1 September 2026 a licensed restaurant caught overcharging faces a multi-day suspension, though open street stalls fall outside that law. Read the posted price before you point, and bring cash. Roughly, food alleys run 09:00 to 23:00 seven days; fabric halls 09:00 to 18:00, closed Sundays.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay per dish. Individual snacks run roughly 3,000–8,000 ₩ and many stalls are cash-first. Prices shift, so check the posted price before ordering.
stops.openingHours: Food alleys roughly 09:00–23:00 daily. General merchandise and fabric halls roughly 09:00–18:00 and closed on Sundays. Hours differ by stall — confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The market floor has no steps at street level, but the food alleys are extremely narrow, crowded and uneven, with bench seating jammed against working stalls. A wheelchair can enter but will not easily move through the aisles at busy times.
stops.insiderTip: Compare the posted price and portion quantity at two or three stalls before you choose — the new labelling rules mean the honest stalls now advertise their weights, so use that. And go easy on the mustard-soy dip at first; it is sharper than it looks.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the market the way you came and walk west along Jongno for about fifteen minutes to Jongno 3-ga. At the big junction, cross and head north up Donhwamun-ro, the street climbing toward the palace. After a couple of minutes, turn into the narrow alleys on your left: that tangle of low tiled roofs is Ikseon-dong.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bgag, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ikseon-dong Hanok Alley
stops.narration:
Ikseon-dong is a knot of tiny alleys packed with hanok, traditional Korean houses with timber frames under heavy grey-tiled roofs, and almost everything you have been told about it being an ancient village is wrong. It is not Joseon. It is a 1920s property development. In the late 1920s and early 1930s a Korean developer named Jeong Se-gwon bought large, old aristocratic estates here, including the former Nudong Palace, a private residence of an earlier king's family, demolished them, and built dozens of small, standardised hanok to sell and rent to working- and middle-class Korean families. He was also making a counter-move: Japanese settlers were expanding north, and dense Korean housing in the centre was a way of holding ground. The alleys are narrow because narrow alleys fit more houses.

So this is Seoul's oldest surviving hanok district, older than the Bukchon most visitors go to instead, and it survived largely by accident. Through the 1990s it was a quiet, ageing, working-class neighbourhood that developers kept trying and failing to demolish. What saved it was coffee: from about 2014, young tenants rented the empty houses and turned them into cafés, bakeries and bars, keeping the old roof beams and tiled courtyards. By 2018, when the city designated the area a Hanok Preservation District, it had become one of the most photographed places in Seoul, and many of the original residents had gone, priced out.

There is no ticket and nothing to queue for; it is a small residential block and people live in it, so keep your voice down and do not photograph into doorways. A café coffee costs roughly 5,000 to 7,000 won. The lanes are flat but the paving is uneven, so wheelchairs and strollers will struggle. Come on a weekday if you can: on weekend afternoons these alleys are shoulder to shoulder.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander. Cafés and restaurants are at normal Seoul prices; a coffee is roughly 5,000–7,000 ₩. Verify at the door.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times as a public neighbourhood; individual cafés and shops keep their own hours, typically late morning to late evening, and some close one weekday. Weekday mornings are the quietest.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free. Narrow, uneven stone-and-paving alleys with occasional thresholds and steps, and passages too tight for a wheelchair or a wide stroller. There is no accessible route through the district.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the whole tangle before you sit anywhere — it takes ten minutes and the density is the point — and look up at the rooflines: the sameness of the small houses is the evidence that this was mass-produced housing, not an old village. Keep your camera pointed at buildings, not doorways.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back out of the alleys to the main road and walk south, crossing back over Jongno. Turn right (west) and follow Jongno for about five minutes until you reach a small, fenced park set back from the street on your right, with a stone pagoda visible through the railings. That is Tapgol Park.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: S h y numis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tapgol Park
stops.narration:
This small, fenced, slightly shabby park is the most political piece of ground on this walk. Its name means "pagoda alley." The grey stone tower behind the railing is the Wongaksa Pagoda, carved in 1467, ten storeys with a bronze finial. It is National Treasure number two, nearly all that is left of Wongaksa, a great Buddhist temple established here in the 1460s by King Sejo. Note the twist: the same Confucian dynasty that built Jongmyo for its ancestors also had a king who founded a Buddhist temple and this pagoda. Sejo had taken the throne from his young nephew and had him killed, and he needed heaven's endorsement, so he bought it with temples.

Now the part that matters most. On 1 March 1919, thirty-three Korean leaders signed a Declaration of Independence and read it aloud in a restaurant beside this park while thousands gathered here. At about two o'clock, someone stood up in the octagonal pavilion, Palgakjeong, built around 1900 as a music hall, and read the declaration to the crowd. Then the crowd walked out into Jongno shouting "Manse!" — "ten thousand years," the traditional Korean cheer for long life, and by that afternoon a cry for independence. Japan had ruled Korea since 1910. The protest spread across the country and was put down hard. It failed, and it also produced the Korean Provisional Government in Shanghai a month later.

Find the statue of Son Byeong-hui, leader of Cheondogyo, a Korean religion blending Confucianism, Buddhism and Christianity, and one of the organisers of the declaration, and the memorial panels carrying the names of the thirty-three signatories. It is free and open daily, roughly 09:00 to 18:00 in the warmer months and 09:00 to 17:00 in winter. The paths are paved and level, so it is one of the most accessible stops; walk softly.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, no ticket and no closing day. It is a public memorial park; donations are not expected.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 09:00–18:00 from March to October and 09:00–17:00 in winter — confirm the gate hours on the day.
stops.accessibility: Mostly step-free and paved, with level paths and abundant benches; a gentle slope in places. The most accessible stop on this walk.
stops.insiderTip: Read the memorial panels by the entrance that list the thirty-three signatories — then look at the men playing janggi on the benches behind you. The contrast is the whole country in one frame. Look for the pagoda's carved railings and dragons up close.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park, turn right (west) and walk along Jongno for about five minutes. On your right, standing on a raised island in the middle of the road, you come to a small pavilion with a large bronze bell. That is Bosingak, at Jonggak subway station.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bosingak Bell Pavilion
stops.narration:
You are standing at the centre of Joseon's clock. The pavilion on the traffic island is Bosingak, the bell pavilion, and the street you are on is named after it: Jongno means "bell street." Seoul, then called Hanyang, was ringed by a stone wall whose gates shut at ten each night and opened at four in the morning. The bell was struck 28 times to close the gates and 33 times to open them; the dawn ritual was called paru, the lifting of the night curfew. After the evening bell, only people with official permission could move inside the walls.

The bell you see is not the original. The first great bell here was cast in 1468, in the reign of King Sejo, and eventually cracked beyond ringing; the genuine article sits in the National Museum of Korea as a designated treasure, and this is a replica cast through public donations and hung in 1985. The two-storey pavilion is a 1980 rebuild. The last regular tollings were in 1895, the year Emperor Gojong renamed the tower Bosingak, after electric trams began running through the South Gate, which now had to stay open, and cheap clocks made the service unnecessary. The bell fell silent in 1908 for forty-five years.

Then in 1953, with the Korean War barely stopped, the city rebuilt the tower and rang it again, turning the ringing into what it is now: at midnight on 31 December, thirty-three strikes, because thirty-three was the count that once opened the city gates at dawn. Ordinary citizens joined the ceremony from 1986. There is no ticket and you cannot go inside; you look at it from the pavement, level and step-free, reached by the crossings at Jonggak subway station (exit 4). If you are here for New Year's Eve, come hours early; Line 1 trains skip Jonggak station at midnight.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The pavilion is viewed from the street and cannot be entered. The New Year's Eve ceremony is free and open to all.
stops.openingHours: Visible from the street at all hours. The New Year's Eve bell-ringing ceremony is held on 31 December around midnight; roads around the pavilion close from the evening, so arrive early.
stops.accessibility: Level pavement and crossings; step-free to view from the street. The pavilion itself is raised and not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Come back on the evening of 31 December if you are here for the New Year — the bell is struck 33 times at midnight and the crowd is enormous; get there by early evening. On an ordinary day, imagine the count: the same thirty-three strikes that once opened the city's gates at dawn are the ones you hear at midnight.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Jongno to the south side and walk a short way west to where the street bridges the water. Take the steps down to the streamside walkway and follow the water west, below street level, for about ten minutes. The channel opens into a plaza with a tall, spiral sculpture standing in the water: that is Cheonggye Plaza, the head of the stream.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Richard Mortel, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Cheonggyecheon Stream
stops.narration:
You are standing at the head of a stream that spent thirty years as a motorway. The water running west to east below street level is the Cheonggyecheon, and the sculpture in it, a twenty-metre painted-steel spiral, is "Spring," by Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen, installed in 2006.

It drains the Suseongdong valley on Inwangsan and runs about eleven kilometres to the Han River. From 1958 the channel was covered with concrete to make a road, and in 1976 the elevated Cheonggye Overpass opened above it, a deck of more than five kilometres carrying 170,000 vehicles a day. By 2001, engineers found cracked concrete and load capacity it could no longer carry. Lee Myung-bak, mayor from 2002, made daylighting the stream his signature project: work ran from July 2003 to September 2005, around 620,000 tonnes of concrete and asphalt came down, 5.8 kilometres of channel were rebuilt with 22 bridges, and the stream reopened on 1 October 2005. The bill was 386.7 billion won, about 280 million US dollars then and above the 349 billion budgeted.

Supporters call it a triumph: a motorway replaced by a linear park, a corridor measurably cooler in summer. Critics call it theatre: the natural flow is too small, so tens of thousands of tonnes a day are pumped in from the Han River and from subway groundwater, treated and held at a steady forty centimetres, at a cost of billions of won a year. Several thousand street traders were moved out, first to the old Dongdaemun Stadium site, then to Sinseol-dong when the stadium was demolished, and many say their trade never recovered. The path is free around the clock, but in rain or heavy snow sections close, and this water rises fast: never shelter under the bridges. It is not step-free everywhere; the accessible ramp is here at Cheonggye Plaza.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open around the clock. No ticket; sections may be closed after heavy rain or snow for safety.
stops.openingHours: The walkway is open 24 hours, seven days a week, but access is restricted during and after heavy rain or snow. The Seoul Lantern Festival lights the stream in late autumn into winter — check the dates if your visit overlaps.
stops.accessibility: Partly step-free: Cheonggye Plaza has an accessible ramp down to the water, but most other crossings reach the walkway by stairs only, and the path can be icy in winter. Wheelchair users should plan to use the plaza end.
stops.insiderTip: Walk at least a few hundred metres of the channel, not just the plaza — the point of the stream is the noise dropping away as you go below street level. If it is icy, stay off the frozen margins and use the street-level pavements, dropping back down where the path is clear.
stops.nextStopDirections: Climb back up from the stream and cross the wide avenue (Sejong-daero) to the north side, then walk north for a few minutes, following the line of the avenue. Ahead of you, at the foot of a large seated bronze statue, the buildings open out into a long public square: Gwanghwamun Square.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gwanghwamun Square
stops.narration:
You finish at Korea's front yard. Behind the gate in front of you, Gwanghwamun, "the gate of broad light," is Gyeongbokgung, the palace the Joseon kings built in 1395 and then abandoned for two and a half centuries after Japan's invasion burned it in 1592. The gate was rebuilt in 1867, pushed aside by the Japanese colonial government to make room for its own headquarters, reconstructed in concrete in the 1960s, and rebuilt again in wood, in its original position, in 2010.

This square was Yukjo-geori, the Street of the Six Ministries. Its modern life is as the country's protest stage: hundreds of thousands have filled it, most dramatically in 2016 and 2017, when the candlelight vigils here helped force the impeachment of President Park Geun-hye.

King Sejong the Great, seated with a book, invented hangul, the Korean alphabet, in the 1440s, a writing system simple enough for ordinary people to learn. The taller figure is Admiral Yi Sun-sin, raised in 1968: the admiral who destroyed a far larger Japanese fleet at Myeongnyang in 1597 with thirteen ships. The square is new: closed for twenty-one months, reopened in August 2022, roughly doubled in size by shutting the western traffic lanes and planting thousands of trees, and its woldae, the raised platform where the king once stood for ceremonies, was rebuilt. In winter it hosts an illumination festival, with a public ice rink at Seoul Plaza nearby. So that is old Seoul, walked end to end: a shrine where kings are still ritually fed, a 1905 market still frying mung beans, hanok lanes a developer built and baristas saved, a park where independence was declared, a bell that once shut the city's gates, and a stream dug out beneath a motorway. The argument is the same at every stop: what to keep, what to tear down, who decides.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public square. The palace behind the gate charges separately (Gyeongbokgung around 3,000 ₩ for adults, closed Tuesdays); verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; best after dark in winter for the lights. Gyeongbokgung Palace behind the gate keeps its own hours and closes on Tuesdays.
stops.accessibility: Flat, wide and step-free throughout, with benches, ramps and subway entrances on the square. The most accessible stop on the walk.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the admiral's statue and look back north: the Woldae, the restored stone platform, and the mountains behind the gate line up — this is the view the square was rebuilt for. Then look at the empty lanes where traffic used to run, and remember this was a road until 2022.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. You are on Gwanghwamun Square with Gyeongbokgung Palace behind the gate ahead of you. Subway stations (Gwanghwamun on Line 5, Gyeongbokgung on Line 3) are on either side of the square, and the stream where you finished earlier is two blocks south. If you still have appetite after all that market food, the alleys of Insa-dong and the hanok cafés of Seochon are a short walk west and north.
